oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Improving Special Education Decision-Making Through Structured Deliberation: IDEA, Section 504, and Texas ARD Procedures
oai_dc:dc.dc:creator: Brazell, Nathan
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Abstract Special education law depends on collaborative, individualized decision-making, yet the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), Section 504, and Texas Admission, Review, and Dismissal (ARD) procedures often leave teams without a disciplined method for addressing material disagreements before conflict escalates into formal dispute resolution. This policy brief examines statutory, regulatory, and judicial requirements governing parental participation, open-minded decision-making, consideration of alternatives, and reasoned documentation. It argues that public school systems should incorporate structured deliberation into individualized education program and ARD meetings—and comparable Section 504 meetings—when a material disagreement emerges. The proposed five-step protocol requires teams to define the disputed issue, identify the governing legal or educational criterion, connect proposals to relevant evidence, test reasonable alternatives, and record the decision and its reasons. Existing research on parent-school conflict and alternative dispute resolution supports these process targets, although it does not establish that the proposed protocol will reduce disputes. Texas’s collaborative ARD requirements, recess procedure, and expanded IEP-facilitation framework provide a particularly suitable implementation context. With safeguards against delay and coercion, structured deliberation offers a practical method for improving decision quality, participant understanding, and the legal record before formal proceedings become necessary. Keywords: special education, structured deliberation, IDEA, Section 504, ARD committees, dispute resolution
